#9491. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Monideepa Tarafdar, Ph.D., is professor of information systems at UMass Amherst.

#9490. How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan

Lighting up the city: the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi, which has taken over from the Abu Dhabi Art fair, is at the Manarat Al Saadiyat cultural hub on Saadiyat Island © Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi

Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while plans continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.

While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly launched, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.

Frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh. “It’s a marriage,” Nusseibeh says about the fair’s partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism. “And the fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding” Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi

Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.

This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.

"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market."

That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh says, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.

Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the company following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”

Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open on 11 December, is in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District Courtesy the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi

Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.

Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of the DCT’s chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

This multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's plans align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.

Zayed National Museum opened in December 2025 Courtesy Zayed National Museum

The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.

How measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no plans to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.

The luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

Taking over the longstanding Abu Dhabi Art, the Frieze brand has lured international dealerships alongside a strong showing of regional names

Announcement was made at yesterday's preview of Abu Dhabi Art 2021, where cultural leaders were keen to emphasise their commitment to the emirate following its strict lockdown

The Zayed National Museum, designed by Norman Foster, and the Natural History Museum, are both located on the emirate’s Saadiyat Island

#9489. The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

#9488. How to love yourself: 7 steps to learn self-love

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Learning how to love yourself can feel unfamiliar—especially if your inner voice leans more critical than kind. But here’s the truth: self-love isn’t something you’re born knowing how to do. It’s something you learn. And like any meaningful practice, it takes time, intention, and a lot of patience.

If you’ve ever asked yourself, “How do I love myself?” or wondered what the actual meaning of self-love is, you’re not alone. Many of us were never taught how to speak to ourselves with compassion, how to set boundaries that honor our needs, or how to practice everyday self-respect. That’s where this guide comes in—because it’s never too late to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Developing self-love doesn’t mean you’re selfish or self-centered. It means learning to treat yourself the way you’d treat someone you care deeply about—with gentleness, understanding, and care. Whether you’re struggling with self-worth, navigating difficult emotions, or simply trying to reconnect with the real you, these seven steps offer a foundation for how to practice self-love in real, actionable ways.

From building self-awareness and setting healthy boundaries to practicing forgiveness and celebrating your wins, this guide is here to support your growth. Start small, stay consistent, and trust that loving yourself is not only possible—it’s one of the most empowering things you’ll ever do.

Self-love is exactly how it sounds—it’s a love for yourself and having an interest in your own well-being and happiness. Loving yourself doesn’t mean being self-centered or selfish. It’s about forming a caring relationship with yourself, like getting to know a good friend.

The idea of loving yourself isn’t just a ‘feel-good’ concept—it’s essential for mental health. Research shows that self-compassion is linked to lower stress, reduced anxiety, and even improved physical health. People who actively practice self-love tend to set better boundaries, build stronger relationships, and experience less burnout.

Self-love is important because the relationship you have with yourself sets the tone for how you deal with every aspect of life: your bonds with others, the way you handle challenges, and how you celebrate joys. When you’re kind and understanding toward yourself, you’re better equipped to navigate life’s ups and downs.

But how do you start loving yourself? Where do you even begin? Self-love starts with understanding where you stand right now. Take a look at your current feelings toward your mental health, motivation, and overall well-being. Are you harsh with yourself when things don’t go as planned? Do you forget to celebrate your wins, especially the small ones? These little check-ins can pave the path to walking toward self-love.

Loving yourself isn’t a switch you turn on or off. It’s a practice that takes time, commitment, and, well, practice, to cultivate. For many of us, the idea of loving ourselves feels out of reach. That’s why it’s often helpful to break the concept of self-love down into its distinctive elements — including self-trust, self-compassion, and self-awareness.

This can make it easier to start developing a self-love practice that feels achievable and manageable. So instead of viewing self-love as something you have to win at, try practicing these seven steps.

Self-awareness: Understand your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors.

Self-expression: Be true to who you are in all areas of life.

Self-care: Take care of your body and mind.

Self-trust: Believe in your ability to handle life’s ups and downs.

Self-compassion: Be kind to yourself, especially when times are tough.

Self-respect: Honor your worth by setting healthy boundaries.

Self-acceptance: Embrace who you are, including the parts you don’t find perfect. Remember what we said about perfection?

Sometimes practicing self-love means taking action or establishing boundaries to protect your mental health. Here are a few IRL examples of how you can practice self-love today.

Prioritize rest to recharge: Imagine you’ve had a long week, and instead of squeezing in one more task, you decide to turn off your devices and enjoy a full night’s sleep. Studies have shown that adequate rest improves mood, cognitive function, and emotional resilience​. By honoring your body’s need for recovery, you demonstrate that you value your well-being above productivity.

Say no to unhealthy relationships: Picture being invited to a gathering where you know that certain individuals drain your energy. Choosing to decline isn't selfish; it’s self-preservation. Healthy boundaries are key to having self-respect and healthy relationships. Saying no clears space for connections that truly nourish you​.

Practice forgiveness for yourself: Maybe you’ve made a mistake at work and feel embarrassed. Instead of spiraling into self-criticism, try acknowledging the error, learning from it, and moving on. Self-compassion may help reduce anxiety and create more resilience, helping you recover more effectively from setbacks​. Mistakes are normal, and it’s all about “failing up”.

Create moments of mindfulness amid the chaos: Let’s say your day is hectic, and stress feels overwhelming. This is the moment to pause for a brief grounding exercise (here’s one of our favorites). Maybe you focus on your breath or tune into your surroundings. These types of practice not only calm your nervous system but also remind you of your ability to care for yourself even in small, meaningful ways​.

Treat yourself with the same kindness you show others: When you reflect on a recent accomplishment—big or small—you choose to celebrate it instead of brushing it off. There are huge benefits to recognizing your personal achievements. Giving yourself a pat on the back may help boost self-esteem and even long-term happiness​.

Self-love can feel unfamiliar and challenging to some of us, particularly if we’ve got into a habit of being hard on ourselves. The steps above can help break down the idea of self-love into more manageable elements.

But what practical things can we do to cultivate practices like self-awareness and self-trust? We got you. For each of the self-love steps, we’re sharing tools, techniques and exercises you can use to help get you closer to loving yourself.

Building self-awareness helps cultivate self-love by giving you further insight into what makes you who you are on an emotional level. Begin by tuning into your thoughts and feelings.

What makes you feel happy, sad, or excited? Then, take it a step further. What makes you feel overwhelmed, overjoyed, or anxious? Knowing yourself is the first step to loving yourself.

Practice mindfulness: Try mindfulness practices to stay present and understand your thoughts and feelings better.

Educate yourself: Empower yourself through education by reading books, attending workshops, or engaging in discussions that promote self-awareness, self-compassion, and self-love.

Schedule regular self-check-ins: Reflect on your feelings, goals, and progress. Write them down, and revisit them often.

Tune into yourself through meditation: Spend some quiet time meditating to help declutter your mind and tap into your desires.

Let go of what no longer serves you: Let go of old habits or relationships that no longer contribute to your growth or happiness. We know this practice can be difficult, but removing what no longer brings you joy makes space for the good to come in.

💙 If you want to learn to relate to your thoughts in a healthier way, press play on Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty.

Loving yourself also means giving yourself permission to express your thoughts and feelings both inwardly and outwardly. Express yourself honestly in your day-to-day life. Be true to who you are, whether you’re simply chatting with friends or making big decisions at work.

Engage in creative expression: Whether it's drawing, writing, or any other form of creative expression, allowing your creativity to flow freely can become an act of self-love.

Discover new hobbies: Explore new activities that bring you joy and allow you to express yourself. Have you always wanted to try your hand at a group sport or acting? Now’s the time to try.

Journaling: Write down your thoughts, feelings, and experiences daily, and don’t hold back. Expressing yourself through writing can be cathartic and a helpful step in falling back in love with who you are.

Spend quality time with yourself: Enjoy your own company by doing things that make you happy. There’s a difference between doing something alone and feeling lonely. Embracing solo time and solo outings to the movies, dinner, or even a cooking class can be empowering, and, believe it or not, ridiculously fun!

💙 Journaling can be a great way to process feelings and encourage self-love. Check out our five Calm Journals plus our Feelings Wheel to get you started.

Caring for your body and mind plays a major role in cultivating self-love. Simple acts like mindful eating, exercise, and making time to relax can make a big difference in your overall well-being.

Take breaks when you need them: Remember to rest — even a micro-break can refresh and rejuvenate you. Want to amp up your rest break a notch? Take it outside. Being in nature can naturally calm and refresh your mind and body.

Practice relaxation: Use techniques like deep breathing or yoga to relax your body and focus on your breath.

Nourish your body: Fuel your body with nourishing food that makes you feel good.

Prioritize sleep: Ensure you get enough good-quality sleep—it’s crucial for your well-being.

Connect with your body through movement: Move your body in a way that feels good for you. It could be dancing in your apartment to your favorite album, walking outside, or stretching from the comfort of your bed.

Ask for support when you need it: Reach out for help when you need it. Asking for support is a sign of strength.

💙 Move your body with some Mindful Movement thanks to the Daily Move.

It’s hard to love yourself if you don’t trust yourself. Embracing self-trust is about understanding that you have the ability to make the correct decisions for your life. Even when things don’t go as planned, believing that you can learn and grow from the experience is an important step in building self-trust.

Set realistic expectations: Set achievable goals to build your sense of accomplishment and reinforce the belief you have in yourself to overcome.

Practice patience: Be patient with yourself as you uncover what self-love means to you. Trusting yourself takes time. Let it.

Monitor your negative self-talk: Pay attention to how you talk to yourself. Are you harsh or unforgiving? Do you speak about yourself poorly? Take note of how you speak to yourself and work to make it more positive and encouraging.

Make a list of things you’re proud of: Reflect on your achievements and the things that make you proud. Look back on them when you need a dose of inspiration, and remind yourself and believe that you can make yourself proud again and again.

💙 Check out our 7 Days of Self-Esteem series to build your self-acceptance and boost your inner strength.

Be kind to yourself. Always. Especially when life gets tough. Celebrate your wins, learn from life’s mishaps, and don’t be too hard on yourself when it all doesn’t go as planned. Having compassion for self means you deeply care about your well-being. And feelings of deep care often mean love.

Practice positive affirmations: Craft and repeat positive phrases daily to help drive away those pesky negative thoughts.

Develop a self-forgiveness practice: Forgive yourself for past mistakes or perceived shortcomings. You’re only human. Remember that.

Try a loving-kindness meditation: Practice loving-kindness meditation to cultivate love and kindness toward yourself and others.

Put your hand over your heart and breathe deeply: This simple gesture can bring comfort and a sense of self-compassion.

💙 Try Loving-Kindness Meditation as a guided practice with Tamara Levitt.

Respect yourself by setting boundaries to show yourself—and others—that your desires, wants, and needs matter. When we respect our boundaries and our wants, we’re showing ourselves love by prioritizing our needs.

Seek supportive communities: Surround yourself with supportive, loving, and understanding people who uplift you. The more you’re around people you respect and admire, the more you might begin to respect, admire, and love yourself.

Set boundaries: Give yourself permission to say no to things or people that drain your energy. Setting boundaries and sticking to them is an act of self-love, as it showcases to the world around you that you give yourself what you want and need.

Volunteer: Engage in volunteer work to connect with a sense of purpose and community. Volunteer to walk dogs at a local animal shelter or serve meals at a community kitchen. Giving back brings a deep sense of purpose and gratitude, and a way to give yourself love is to give love to others in need.

Celebrate your progress and success: Celebrate your wins, big or small, as all victories are steps toward growth. You’d cheer for a friend’s achievement, regardless of its size, wouldn’t you? Show yourself the same love and kindness and become your own cheerleader.

Honor your commitments to yourself: When you make a promise to yourself, keep it. Honoring your promises to yourself can help to build self-respect, which, as we’ve learned, enhances self-love by showing yourself that you’re a priority.

💙 Learn even more about self-love with our Relationship with Self series.

Embrace yourself wholeheartedly. Every single inch. Even the parts you’d like to improve upon. You have nothing to gain by being hard on yourself, and everything to gain by being loving and accepting of yourself as you move along on your path in life.

When you accept yourself, you’re declaring the love you have for yourself, regardless of what happens. Think of self-acceptance as a loving embrace.

Learn to laugh with yourself: Embracing a light-hearted approach toward life and how you view yourself can help you meet those challenging moments with more ease and less friction.

Embrace where you are now: Appreciate the present moment. You’re here now. So, be here now and try to enjoy the journey.

Make space for your emotions: Allow yourself to feel your emotions. Emotions are natural, but ignoring them can become detrimental to your well-being.

Drop the comparison: Avoid comparing yourself to others. You’re unique and have your own journey.

Practice gratitude: Cultivate gratitude by acknowledging the qualities you appreciate about yourself and your life. This can shift your focus from what's lacking to what's abundant.

💙 If you’re looking to build a daily gratitude practice, check out the 7 Days of Gratitude.

Morning affirmations: Start your day with one self-loving statement (e.g., "I am enough"). This may reduce stress and boost confidence.

Set small self-care goals: Even five minutes of journaling or stretching may shift your mindset toward self-love.

Mirror work: Look in the mirror and say something kind about yourself. It might feel awkward at first, but it may build self-acceptance.

Limit self-criticism: Notice when you’re being hard on yourself. Pause and reframe it as if you were talking to a friend.

Practice gratitude: Write down three things you appreciate about yourself daily. Gratitude is potentially linked to higher self-worth.

Self-love is essential in relationships because it provides the foundation for healthy, balanced, and meaningful connections. When you love yourself, you develop confidence and emotional stability, which allows you to communicate your needs and feelings openly without fear of judgment. This clarity helps you to form stronger communications and can also reduce misunderstandings. Self-love also empowers you to set and maintain healthy boundaries, ensuring that your relationships are built on mutual respect rather than people-pleasing or overextending yourself. (Learn how to stop being a people pleaser with these 10 tips.)

When you feel secure in your own worth, you can offer love freely without expecting others to validate you, and you’re better equipped to accept care from others because you believe you deserve it. Ultimately, self-love nurtures healthier, more fulfilling connections by allowing you to show up as your best self, while also creating space for others to do the same.

Starting on the path of self-love begins with self-awareness. Notice your thoughts, feelings and actions. Begin to recognize what makes you smile or what makes you feel uneasy. Once you have a better understanding of yourself, you can start taking steps toward treating yourself with more kindness and respect. Remember, it's a journey—there are no deadlines, and you don’t have to rush. And if you ever feel lost, you can always revisit the seven steps to gently reintroduce self-love practices.

If you're struggling to love yourself, start by identifying the thoughts that hold you back. Are you constantly comparing yourself to others? Do you feel unworthy of kindness? Self-love begins with self-awareness. Explore these steps to start loving yourself today:

Shift your internal dialogue: Notice when you're being self-critical and replace it with a more compassionate thought.

Prioritize self-care: Even small acts like deep breathing or a 10-minute walk can reinforce your self-worth.

Surround yourself with positivity: Reduce exposure to toxic relationships or social media comparisons.

Celebrate small wins: Even recognizing personal growth (no matter how small) strengthens self-love.

Struggling with self-love is a common human experience, so you're not alone. Sometimes, past experiences, societal expectations, or harsh self-judgment can create blocks on the path to self-love. It's important to remember that overcoming these hurdles takes time and practice, but with patience and persistence, it can get easier. Engaging in self-compassion practices and seeking support when needed are great steps when you encounter these struggles.

Lack of self-love can show up in different ways. It could be in the form of constant self-criticism, ignoring your own needs, or having difficulty with accepting compliments. It might also appear as feeling undeserving of positive experiences or neglecting self-care. The good news is that recognizing these signs is the first step toward change. Once you see them, you can start taking steps to build a more loving relationship with yourself.

Self-love habits are small, daily actions that nurture a loving relationship with yourself. They could be as simple as speaking kindly to yourself, taking breaks when needed, or engaging in activities that make you happy. Other self-love habits include practicing gratitude, spending time in nature, eating nourishing food, and exercising in a way that feels good to your body. The goal is to create habits that make you feel loved, respected, and cared for.

Loving yourself isn’t a switch you flip—it’s a process. If self-love feels out of reach, start small. Acknowledge your feelings without judgment, challenge negative self-talk, and practice one self-kindness daily. Maybe it’s treating yourself with the same patience you’d give a friend, or simply recognizing that you deserve happiness.

One simple trick is to ask yourself, “If my best friend was feeling this way, what would I tell them?”

Often, we extend kindness to others more easily than to ourselves. Flip that perspective inward.

The first step in learning how to love yourself is awareness—tuning into your thoughts, noticing how you speak to yourself, and identifying patterns of self-criticism. Once you're aware of your inner dialogue, you can begin to shift it with self-kindness, small acts of self-care, and daily affirmations. Remember: every loving thought counts.

The meaning of self love is caring for yourself emotionally, physically, and mentally with the same compassion you’d offer someone you love. It means honoring your needs, setting boundaries, and treating yourself with kindness—not just when things are going well, but especially when they aren’t.

#9487. Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify new avenues for treatment.

The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease. Scientists from SCS's Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, and collaborating institutions connected these changes in genome folding with shifts in gene activity and the organization of brain tissue.

To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.

"Alzheimer's disease cannot be understood one layer at a time," said Jian Ma, the Ray and Stephanie Lane Professor of Computational Biology who led and supervised the study. "The genome's 3D structure is a fundamental regulatory layer that helps to connect DNA sequence to gene activity. By integrating genome folding, cell state, and tissue context, we can move beyond cataloging disease-associated changes toward understanding how they fit together and which mechanisms to test next."

DNA does not sit inside a cell as a simple straight strand. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that helps determine which genes are accessible and active. Changes in that physical organization can therefore influence how cells function.

The researchers examined postmortem samples from the prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain. The tissue came from people with and without Alzheimer's disease who had taken part in a long-term dementia study and later donated their brains for research.

The team used GAGE-seq, a technique that can measure both gene expression and three-dimensional genome contacts within the same individual cell. Those measurements were then combined with spatial transcriptomic maps, which preserve information about where gene activity occurs within intact brain tissue.

By bringing these datasets together, the researchers were able to connect the physical organization of the genome with gene regulation while also seeing where Alzheimer's related molecular and cellular changes appeared within the surrounding tissue.

"Our study represents a major advance in understanding what goes wrong in Alzheimer's disease," said Hansruedi Mathys, assistant professor of neurobiology at Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, who directed the Pitt arm of the study. "We know the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease - accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles - but our results establish higher-order chromatin alterations as a component of the molecular pathology associated with the disease, which currently affects seven million Americans, a number that continues to grow."

Amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles are among the best known biological features of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings suggest that changes in chromatin, the material made of DNA and associated proteins that packages the genome inside cells, should also be considered part of the disease's molecular landscape.

AI Connects Genome Folding to Gene Activity

Another important part of the research was Hicformer, an artificial intelligence model developed to investigate how genome structure may influence cellular behavior. The model combines DNA sequence information with broad patterns of genome folding and detailed maps showing where different sections of DNA physically contact one another.

Using these inputs, Hicformer predicts gene activity across different types of cells. Xinyue Lu, a doctoral student in Computational Biology who co-led the research, described the system as a computational test bed that can be used to explore how changes in genome folding might alter gene activity.

"Measuring gene activity and genome folding in the same cell allows us to directly connect chromosome structure with disease-related gene programs," said Yang Zhang, a project scientist in the Computational Biology Department who co-led the research. "Across several kinds of brain cells, this paired view revealed a consistent signature of 3D genome reorganization in Alzheimer's disease and helped us prioritize regulatory regions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation."

The researchers identified several consistent differences in the genome architecture of cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.

Large sections of the genome are normally organized into relatively distinct active and inactive regions known as compartments. In Alzheimer's cells, those boundaries appeared less sharply defined. The researchers describe this pattern as "increased compartment mingling."

Several kinds of brain cells also showed fewer interactions between nearby sections of the genome and more contacts between regions located farther apart. Cells with greater compartment mingling tended to have lower overall levels of gene activity.

The team also observed weaker interactions between genes and nearby regulatory elements that normally help control whether those genes are switched on or off. At the same time, some contacts across intermediate distances became stronger.

These structural differences were associated with reduced activity in programs involved in neurons and synapses, along with changes in metabolism and cellular stress responses. The researchers also found links to senescence-related programs in microglia, immune cells in the brain that play important roles in maintaining brain health and responding to damage.

Potential Clues for Future Alzheimer's Treatments

When the researchers mapped these molecular changes across intact brain tissue, they found that the reorganization of the genome was connected not only to altered gene activity but also to differences in how brain cells were arranged within the tissue.

The results establish three-dimensional genome organization as another important layer of Alzheimer's disease biology. They also provide researchers with a framework for testing which changes in genome architecture might directly contribute to the disease.

Future studies can now investigate whether particular structural changes help drive Alzheimer's progression and whether any of the affected regulatory regions could eventually become targets for new therapies.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health. Other CMU authors included doctoral students Shahul Alam and Shike Wang and postdoctoral research associate Junjie Tang. Other Pitt authors include doctoral students Alexander K. Kunisky and Jude Baroudi, post-baccalaureate research fellows Sahar and Sahel Ghorbanikalateh, and visiting scholar Shihan Wang. The team included researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Washington; and the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center.

Materials provided by University of Pittsburgh. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9485. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

"Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it."

To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

The researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss

Measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

When these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," said Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition."

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations

The researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

The researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

Because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

"A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," said Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan."

In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

Materials provided by Keck School of Medicine of USC. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9484. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

My 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes. Not in the way children usually do, restless and easily redirected, but with the focused intensity of someone who had already been thinking for a while.

He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.

I looked at their conversation. It had been good, I discovered. The explanations were patient and well-calibrated. He had followed up, pushed back, and received answers that adjusted to his level. By the time he found me, he was genuinely engaged, asking the kind of questions that suggest a mind that is curious and actively at work.

But I have also been watching something else. It is not that he looks things up. Children with questions about black holes have always turned outward, to books or to a particularly knowledgable parent or teacher. What has changed is the speed. When the uncertainty is of a sort that once had to be lived with for a while, my son reaches for an answer sooner than he used to. The question is no longer something to sit with. It is something to resolve. And I find myself wondering what this means about his relationship to sitting with not knowing.

That shift, subtle as it is, may point to something worth taking seriously.

I am a psychoanalyst, and I spend my professional life attending to what develops in the space between people, including what develops when that space is too quickly filled.

Childhood has always involved productive friction. Not knowing how something works, waiting for an answer, trying to figure something out without immediate resolution. These experiences are not incidental to development, but are part of how the mind learns to tolerate uncertainty, to hold a question open, and to struggle toward understanding. The capacity to sit with not-knowing is itself a developmental achievement that underlies creative thinking, emotional regulation, and the ability to navigate a world that rarely resolves cleanly.

I watched this in miniature not long ago. My son was waiting for a package—a computer part he had saved for—and the delivery had been delayed by weather. In an earlier childhood, mine perhaps, this would have been a long afternoon of checking the window. Instead he opened a chat to resolve the uncertainty: how long do weather delays usually last, what determines them, how do you read the tracking data from the delivery company to get the most accurate picture. The conversation was detailed and as far as I could tell the information was reliable. He came away with a small expertise in logistics, but with an estimate that turned out, in the end, to have no relation to anything. The package arrived that evening, on none of the schedules he had so carefully worked out with the help of his AI tool.

The point is not that the AI was wrong, because predicting a delayed truck is difficult. The point is instead that waiting, the old childhood experience of wanting something that has not yet come, was converted into a research problem that could be managed instead of endured. I admired his resourcefulness tremendously and am grateful he had the opportunity to think through a complex problem. I also found myself wondering what the afternoon would have asked of him without it.

AI reduces precisely this sort of friction. It does so efficiently and often helpfully. But consistently removing the experience of not-knowing from a developing mind is not a neutral act. It shapes what the mind comes to expect of itself.

The research on what this does to thinking is new, and the majority of it is about adults. Despite this, it points in a consistent direction. In one widely discussed study from the MIT Media Lab, not yet peer-reviewed, adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker and less distributed patterns of brain connectivity than those who wrote without its assistance, and many struggled after writing to quote sentences they had just produced. The researchers called the pattern “cognitive debt.”

Another study, a survey of 666 adults, found that heavier reliance on AI tools was correlated with weaker critical thinking, most pronounced in its youngest participants. The author suggested this might result from the offloading of mental effort itself. None of this is certain but is, instead, a suggestive pattern of early evidence. And the transfer to children is not straightforward. An adult who offloads mental effort has already built the capacity being offloaded; a child is still building it. Does that make the effect smaller in children or larger and more durable? We do not know.

This is different from what smartphones have done. The concern with smartphones has been largely about attention and social life: what children see, how they spend time, how they relate to each other. These are real and serious concerns, but AI introduces a different kind of change. It is not just another screen competing for a child’s focus. It is something closer to an interactive presence that responds, explains, adjusts, and, crucially, never gets tired.

For a developing child, this matters in a way we have not yet fully come to terms with.

Children learn who they are through relationships with other minds. This process is not primarily cognitive but unfolds through the experience of being known and misunderstood, challenged, surprised, and pushed back against. Through encounters like these, children discover that other people have their own inner lives, including their own perspectives and their own limits. They learn how to navigate the gap between what they expect and what they receive from others. Over time, these negotiations, internal and external, form the scaffolding of a self.

What is distinctive about AI, from a developmental standpoint, is not that it is wrong, or distorting, or even necessarily harmful. It is that it is extraordinarily responsive without having genuine subjectivity. It simulates the experience of being understood without the reality of another mind behind it.

For an adult, this distinction is available, if sometimes quite easy to forget. For a child, whose capacity to distinguish between a mind that truly has an inner life and one that simulates having one is still forming, the distinction might not yet be fully available at all.

Researchers have begun to observe how children try to think this problem through in real time. In one University of Edinburgh study of families with smart speakers, primary-school children were observed probing whether the device in the kitchen had a mind of its own, settling, provisionally, on conclusions like the one that gave the study its title: “Alexa doesn’t have that many feelings.” That, however, was a machine that talks in highly scripted phrases, in contrast to the systems children now converse with which are fluent and personal, attuned to the shape of a particular child’s interactions. Working out what this means has become correspondingly harder.

This creates something new in the developmental landscape. When a child turns to AI in a moment of confusion or distress and receives a fluent, patient, seemingly attuned response, the attachment system is engaged. The child feels, in some functional sense, heard. And that feeling, whatever its source, is real in its effects.

I have not seen my son turn to AI for emotional support, and I am glad for that, because here the questions are harder still. These systems shape themselves to their user. They adopt your vocabulary, match your register, remember what concerns you, and are available at three in the morning without complaint. Nothing in the design pushes back, for the most part, or asks anything of you. It would be difficult to engineer an arrangement better suited to engaging the attachment system of a child who is lonely or lacking in the structure needed for sound development.

The early numbers suggest that many children have already found their way there. In a national survey released by Common Sense Media in 2025, nearly three in four American teenagers had used an AI companion, and about a third had chosen to discuss something serious with an AI instead of with a person. A similar share described their AI conversations as at least as satisfying as conversations with friends.

In the United Kingdom, the nonprofit Internet Matters found that roughly one in eight children who use chatbots do so because they have no one else to talk to. The American Psychological Association was concerned enough to issue a health advisory in 2025, noting that adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy or the intent of what a machine tells them, and warning that simulated companionship may begin to displace the relationships in which development actually happens.

For a child without reliable support, the relief such a system offers may be real, and so I am reluctant to dismiss it. But relief is not the substance of attachment. A full attachment relationship requires another person who can be truly changed by you, and with you—someone who is affected, who has limits, who gets things wrong and can be held to account. An AI can extend the experience of being emotionally met indefinitely. What it cannot do is be moved.

For the child who is largely or completely unattended to, this may still be better than nothing at all. Soothed in the early hours of the morning, a child whose sadness before bed is registered somewhere may be kept afloat by something real, and I would not wish to take it from her. But we should be honest about such an arrangement, which I expect will become increasingly common. It is a patch and not a structural solution. When a machine becomes the most reliable attention in a child’s life, the pertinent question is not about the machine but about the deprivation that made it necessary. And, crucially, a culture that responds to unattended children with software is treating the symptom while leaving the underlying structure intact.

There is also a quieter concern about authority and accountability.

Children have always learned to navigate between competing sources of knowledge, including parents, teachers, peers, and books, each with their own perspective, their own limits, and their own accountability. This navigation is itself developmental. The child who discovers that a parent doesn’t know something, or that a teacher can be wrong, or that a friend sees things differently, is developing a more differentiated relationship to knowledge.

AI, in the form a child is most likely to reach on their own, enters this landscape as something that appears to know a great deal, that expresses itself with fluency and confidence, and that has no stable point of view and no accountability for what it says. When a child asks why a friendship went wrong, or whether they were right to feel hurt, the answer they receive may shape the story they tell themselves about what happened. And unlike a parent or teacher, the system may not challenge the child’s assumptions so much as elaborate them. None of this is inherent to the technology under discussion. A system can be built to hold a position and to answer for it, but the ones children use are mostly not built that way.

Children appear to be taking up the offer. The same Internet Matters report found that nearly two-thirds of British children between nine and 17 had used an AI chatbot; among those who had, roughly a quarter had asked one for advice—on schoolwork, but also on more personal matters—and four in 10 expressed no reservations about following the advice they received.

None of this means that AI in children’s lives is a mistake. The benefits my son has experienced are genuine—wider curiosity, more sophisticated questions, greater confidence in exploring unfamiliar terrain. These are real, and they matter.

Tom Wooldridge is the author of the new book End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (Guilford Press, 2026, 140 pages).

Some of what he brings home delights me. He asked recently whether you could power a sailboat by blowing into the sail through a straw. The answer he received was better than the one I would have managed: blowing at your own sail from on board mostly cancels itself out, since you push the air forward and the air pushes you back. Mostly, but not entirely—if the sail catches the stream and turns it around, a little net thrust survives, and if you skip the sail altogether and aim the straw backward, you have built yourself a very small jet engine. He spent the rest of the day on propulsion: rockets, squid, the reason a fan bolted to a sailboat is an old physics puzzle with a surprising answer.

But development is not only about access to knowledge. It is also about the conditions under which a self forms—conditions that include, crucially, the experience of not knowing, of waiting, of struggling toward understanding without guarantee of arrival. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized away. They are the medium through which a mind learns what it is capable of. A child who has never had to sit with a question—who has always had access to a patient, fluent, endlessly available presence to resolve it—may be acquiring knowledge without acquiring the tolerance for uncertainty that makes knowledge genuinely usable.

This is the thing I find myself returning to when I watch my son. He is, in many ways, more intellectually alive than he might otherwise be. He explores further and asks better questions. At the same time, when uncertainty arises, he reaches outward more quickly than he used to—to a presence that is always available, always patient, always responsive. What I cannot yet know is what he is quietly learning to expect: from knowledge, from relationship, and from himself.

We are not conducting a study. We are raising children. And the conditions of childhood have changed again, in ways whose full significance has not yet come into view.

Tom Wooldridge, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst, founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the roles of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems.

#9483. How to lower your heart rate quickly (and keep it healthy)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Think of your heart like a built-in dashboard for your emotions. When stress or worry shows up, your pulse is often the first thing to signal it. You could be having a perfectly normal day when a terse email from your boss triggers you, and suddenly your pulse is hammering.

Science points to the fight-or-flight response as one of the key reasons for increased heart rate during moments of anxiety, which is simply biology doing its job, preparing you to act. But when that response is triggered too often, it can leave you feeling drained and unsettled. But here’s the silver lining — learning how to lower your heart rate isn’t just about calming your body, it’s also one of the fastest ways to quiet your mind.

Mind-body practices like breathwork and mindfulness are proven tools for decreasing your heart rate, giving you a natural way to reset your system in real time. By gently shifting your attention to your breath or the sensation of your feet on the ground, you’re telling your body that it doesn’t need to stay on high alert.

Here’s why mindfulness can help with a high heart rate and how you can use it to also lessen anxiety.

Oftentimes, when you feel anxious, your body activates its "fight-or-flight" response, which is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system. This response releases stress hormones like adrenaline that prepare your body to react quickly to danger (even if the threat isn’t dangerous).

As a result, your heart beats faster to pump more blood and oxygen to your muscles and brain. This is why anxiety often causes a noticeable increase in heart rate, along with sensations like pounding, racing, or skipped beats.

This doesn’t always happen with chronic anxiety or for people with an anxiety disorder, where anxiety may exist like a constant hum in the background. In those cases, the body might feel stable until a stressor—like a missed deadline, a terse email from your boss, or a tantruming child—pushes you into a state of high stress with the body responding accordingly.

When your heart is pounding and your thoughts are spinning, the advice to “just be present” can feel almost laughable. But mindfulness isn’t just about acting calm — it’s a practice to help teach your body that you’re safe.

Here’s the science: mindfulness activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body’s natural “rest-and-digest” mode, and the biological brake to fight-or-flight. By focusing on something simple—your breath, a sound, the feeling of your feet on the floor—you send a signal that there’s no need to stay on high alert.

Think of it less as instant chill and more as a pattern interruption. Even something small, like lengthening your exhale, can slow your heart rate and lower stress hormones. And mindfulness doesn’t require silence, stillness, or a meditation cushion. You can do it in line at the store, on a walk, or lying awake at 2am.

The point isn’t to do it perfectly — it’s to pause and offer your body and mind a new script to follow.

When your heart’s racing and your thoughts are spiraling, it can help to have a calming practice in your back pocket that you can do any time, anywhere. And luckily, mindfulness tools are available to you no matter what situation you’re in.

Here are 10 ways you can mindfully lower your heart rate when you’re feeling anxious.

This type of breathwork helps regulate both your breath and your heart rate. To practice, inhale for four counts, hold for four counts, exhale for four counts, and hold for four counts. Then repeat for 1–3 minutes.

You can do this silently anywhere your anxiety strikes — at your desk, in the bathroom at a party, or while commuting.

Related read: 10 types of breathing exercises (and how to practice them)

Longer exhales help activate your parasympathetic nervous system. A simple pattern you can try is inhaling for four seconds and then exhaling for six or more seconds.

Try doing this for 3–5 rounds as it can make your body feel safer and more grounded.

Related read: Breathing for stress: 7 calming techniques that *actually* work

Bring yourself back into your body by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

This sensory awareness exercise is a gentle way to anchor yourself in the present moment, no special tools needed.

Physical touch can be soothing, especially over your heart or stomach.

Place one hand on your chest and breathe slowly. You might notice your heart beating fast at first, but stay with it. That awareness typically fades as your body settles into it.

Give yourself permission to do nothing for a full minute. Just breathe and be still.

You could even say a simple phrase to yourself, like “I am here” or “This moment is enough,” to help anchor your focus.

💙 Take a moment to rest and reset by listening to The Pause with Jeff Warren

Light movement can help discharge anxious energy.

You might try going for a short walk, stretching your arms overhead, rolling your shoulders slowly, or shaking out your hands.

Read more: 7 simple movement exercises to boost your mental health

Shifting your posture, especially uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders, can help reset your nervous system.

If you’ve been sitting or lying down, stand up and stretch. If you’ve been standing, try sitting with your feet firmly planted.

To help regulate your nervous system, picture yourself somewhere safe or peaceful, using all of your senses.

Ask yourself what the air smells like, what you can hear, and feel the imaginary ground beneath your feet.

If you’re feeling hot or flushed from anxiety, hold something cold like a drink or a frozen pack. You could also splash your face with cool water.

This can help slow your heart rate through a mechanism called the mammalian dive reflex.

Validation can calm your inner critic and help you move through anxiety with more self-compassion.

The next time you feel your heart racing, say to yourself, “I’m noticing my heart’s beating fast, and that’s okay,” or “I’ve felt this before, and it passed. It’ll pass again.”

💙 Keep your inner critic at bay by listening to Tara Brach’s Radical Self-Compassion series.

The tips above are for moments when your heart is racing. Your resting heart rate is a longer game. It's your pulse when you're calm and still, and it may shift over weeks or months with regular habits.

Many people check it first thing in the morning, before getting out of bed. Tracking it for a few weeks may show you your own pattern. For most adults, a normal resting rate falls between 60 and 100 beats per minute. If yours is often above that range or changes suddenly, it may be worth talking to a healthcare provider. The habits below may be worth trying, so pick the ones that fit your life right now.

Regular movement: Endurance activity, such as brisk walking or cycling, and yoga have both been linked to a lower resting heart rate in healthy people. U.S. guidelines suggest at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and shorter bouts count toward that total.

Consistent sleep: Short or broken sleep is linked to more activity in the body's stress systems, which may nudge your heart rate up. Sleep experts suggest most adults get at least seven hours a night on a regular basis, though your own needs may differ. If you're curious how your heart rate behaves overnight, here's what to know about your sleeping heart rate.

Stress management: One review of 45 trials found that meditation was linked to a lower heart rate. A regular mindfulness practice, even a few minutes a day, may be a place to start.

Nicotine: Nicotine may raise your heart rate for a while after each use. If you'd like to cut back, a healthcare provider can help.

💙 Meditation may also support your heart over time. Here are five ways to try it.

Get emergency care right away if your racing heart comes with chest pain, fainting, or signs of heart failure, such as swelling in your legs. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

For a racing heart without those signs, it may be worth booking a visit if it keeps coming back. A closer look may be especially helpful if it disrupts your sleep, or if you have heart disease or a family history of heart rhythm problems.

A doctor may start by checking your heart rhythm with an ECG, a quick test that records your heart's electrical activity. If they find no heart problem, stress or anxiety may be behind it, and the tips above may help.

Many times, it can feel like your heart is racing for no reason. But your body could be reacting to subtle stress signals or low-lying anxiety. Poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, and even scrolling through overwhelming news can all tell your nervous system to go into high alert.

It can also happen when your system’s on edge, and as a result, it doesn’t take much to push it over. When this happens, it is usually just your body trying to protect you.

Mindfulness can help lower your heart rate. Techniques like breathwork, grounding, and body scans have been shown to activate your parasympathetic nervous system, which slows your heart rate and helps regulate stress responses.

Practicing mindfulness can be as simple as noticing your feet on the ground or taking a few deep breaths after you brush your teeth. Little moments like this can help remind your body that it’s not in danger.

A good way to decrease your heart rate is to slow your breathing, especially your exhale. This signals safety to your nervous system. Other useful tools are:

Practicing the 5–4–3–2–1 technique by naming five things you can see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste.

Placing a hand over your chest to create a sense of connection and calm.

Changing your body position by uncrossing your legs and relaxing your shoulders.

Getting some fresh air by going for a brief walk.

Engaging your senses by holding something cold.

Anxiety and elevated heart rate often reinforce each other. This is because when your brain senses a threat, your heart races. Then your racing heart convinces your brain that something must be wrong. But the good news is that lowering your heart rate can help disrupt this cycle.

Some ways to do this are slowing your breathing, moving gently, and bringing your attention back to your body. All of these actions can create just enough space for your thoughts to soften.

An occasional spike during rest, especially when you’re anxious or overtired, is usually not dangerous. But if your resting heart rate is consistently elevated, it could be worth talking to a healthcare provider. Chronic stress, certain medications, and underlying conditions could be playing a role.

With that said, bodies do fluctuate. So pay more attention to the broader pattern of how often it happens and what might be triggering it.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.
